set1.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Cardiovascular assessment.
set1.q: A 70-year-old man has this focused cardiac ultrasound showing the heart in cross-section. Which window is it?
opts: Parasternal short axis

Correct. The parasternal short axis view rotates the probe 90 degrees (marker toward the patient's right hip) and gives a cross-sectional view of the ventricles, with a good view of the mitral and aortic valves.
Apical four chamber
The apical four chamber view shows all four chambers at once, from the apex. A cross-sectional view of the ventricles is the short axis.
Subxiphoid
The subxiphoid view looks through the liver from under the xiphoid. A cross-sectional view of the ventricles is the parasternal short axis.
Parasternal long axis
The long axis view shows the heart lengthwise (right ventricle on top, left ventricle, aorta and left atrium), not in cross-section.

set1.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Pulmonary assessment.
set1.q: A 69-year-old woman with dyspnea is scanned for a pleural effusion and pulmonary edema. Which probe is better for this?
opts: Endocavitary
The endocavitary probe is used inside a body cavity, not on the chest wall. Effusion and edema suit the curvilinear probe.
Curvilinear
Correct. The curvilinear probe is better for pleural effusion, pulmonary edema and pneumonia; the linear probe is better for pneumothorax.
Linear array
The linear probe is better for pneumothorax. Effusion, edema and pneumonia suit the curvilinear probe.
Phased array
The phased array is the cardiac probe, used for the four cardiac windows. Effusion and edema suit the curvilinear probe.

set1.io: Distinguish between focused point-of-care ultrasound and comprehensive ultrasonography.
set1.q: A 47-year-old man in the emergency department has a bedside ultrasound to answer one question, whether there is fluid around his heart. Who interprets this point-of-care study?
opts: The clinician who performs it

Correct. Point-of-care ultrasound is focused, limited and goal directed, and it is interpreted by the provider performing it at the bedside, in real time. That is what separates it from a formal study read later by a radiologist.
A radiologist, hours later

A radiologist interprets traditional (comprehensive) ultrasound, which is performed by a certified sonographer and takes hours to days. This bedside, single-question scan is read by the clinician holding the probe.
A certified sonographer
A certified sonographer performs the comprehensive study; the radiologist then reads it. Neither applies to a focused scan the clinician performs and interprets at the bedside.
A cardiologist after an echo
Nothing in point-of-care ultrasound waits on a specialist's read: it is a real-time answer at the bedside, interpreted by whoever performed it. A formal study can follow if needed.

set1.io: Discuss the role of point-of-care ultrasound as an adjunct to the history and physical examination.
set1.q: A 66-year-old man in the intensive care unit needs a central venous catheter. How does point-of-care ultrasound help?
opts: It guides the needle into the vein

Correct. Procedural point-of-care ultrasound includes central venous catheter insertion, paracentesis and thoracentesis, and vascular uses include central lines and ultrasound-guided intravenous access.
It is not used for procedures
Procedures are one of the common point-of-care applications: central venous catheter insertion, paracentesis and thoracentesis.
It measures the catheter's flow
The procedural role is guidance: finding the vessel and placing the line. Measuring catheter flow is not one of the listed uses.
It replaces the chest film afterward
Replacing later studies is not one of its listed roles. Its procedural role is guiding the insertion itself.

set1.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set1.q: A 58-year-old man's color Doppler shows a vessel segment that is black where it runs straight across the beam. Why?
opts: The vessel is clotted
Loss of color flow can be a feature of a deep vein thrombosis, but a black segment exactly where the vessel crosses the beam is the perpendicular zone.
The segment is a vein
Color does not mean artery or vein: blue and red do not necessarily mean venous and arterial. Black is perpendicular flow.
Flow is toward the probe
Flow toward the probe is red (BART: blue away, red towards). Black is flow perpendicular to the beam.
Flow is perpendicular to the beam
Correct. On color Doppler, flow perpendicular to the beam is black; toward the probe is red and away is blue (BART). Color shows direction and velocity, not artery or vein.

set1.io: Interpret basic point-of-care ultrasound findings by distinguishing normal and abnormal findings.
set1.q: A 28-year-old man with sudden dyspnea has this chest ultrasound, and the arrow marks where the lung pattern meets the chest wall pattern. Finding this point rules in what?
opts: A pneumothorax
Correct. The arrow marks the lung point. In the BLUE (bilateral lung ultrasound in emergency) protocol, abolished lung sliding with an A-profile plus a lung point leads to pneumothorax.
Normal lung
Normal lung slides everywhere and has no edge where sliding starts and stops. The lung point is where a pneumothorax ends.
Pulmonary edema
Pulmonary edema is the B-profile: diffuse B lines with lung sliding present. A lung point leads to pneumothorax.
A pleural effusion
An effusion shows anechoic fluid with the spine visible through it (the spine sign). A lung point is the pneumothorax finding.
set1.alt: Ultrasound image of the chest wall with an arrow

set1.io: Distinguish between focused point-of-care ultrasound and comprehensive ultrasonography.
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman arrives confused and cannot give a history. How does a bedside point-of-care ultrasound fit her evaluation?
opts: It replaces the physical exam
Point-of-care ultrasound is an extension of, and a complement to, the history and physical examination. It does not replace them.
It extends the history and exam

Correct. Point-of-care ultrasound can be an extension of the history and physical examination, often when the patient may not be able to give enough information. It gives real-time answers to diagnostic questions at the bedside.
It is ordered after her workup ends
Being ordered after the evaluation describes traditional, comprehensive ultrasound. Point-of-care scanning happens at the bedside as part of the evaluation.
It should wait for her history
The point is the opposite: when the patient cannot give enough information, a bedside scan can extend the history and physical examination now.

set1.io: Integrate laboratory, imaging, and electrocardiographic findings into clinical decision-making.
set1.q: A 59-year-old man on a surgical ward suddenly develops severe, undifferentiated respiratory distress with a falling oxygen saturation. What is the role of point-of-care ultrasound in his care?
opts: Order a formal study and wait
Waiting hours to days for a comprehensive study suits a stable patient, such as a likely deep vein thrombosis with normal vital signs. His instability is why the bedside scan earns its place.
It replaces his physical examination
Point-of-care ultrasound extends and complements the history and physical examination; it never replaces them.
A bedside answer now, beside the exam

Correct. Point-of-care ultrasound gives real-time answers to diagnostic questions at the bedside, as an extension of the history and physical examination, often when the patient cannot give enough information. An unstable, undifferentiated patient needs that now; formal imaging may follow.
It counts only once a radiologist reads it
The bedside scan is interpreted by the provider performing it, in real time. A radiologist reads the traditional, comprehensive study.

set1.io: Integrate laboratory, imaging, and electrocardiographic findings into clinical decision-making.
set1.q: A 30-year-old man is hypotensive after a fall from height. His bedside EFAST (extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma) exam shows a dark stripe between the liver and kidney. How does this finding fit his evaluation?
opts: It rules out bleeding
A normal right upper quadrant shows liver against kidney with no stripe. A dark stripe is free fluid, the opposite of reassurance.
It shows free fluid in the abdomen

Correct. A dark (anechoic) stripe between the liver and kidney is free fluid in Morison's pouch, found by the right upper quadrant window. In a hypotensive trauma patient, the bedside scan answers the question while the evaluation continues.
It must wait for a radiologist
Point-of-care ultrasound is interpreted by the provider performing it, in real time, and should not delay lifesaving measures.
It shows a pleural effusion
A pleural effusion sits above the diaphragm, with the spine sign. Fluid between the liver and kidney is in the abdomen.

set1.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Soft tissue assessment.
set1.q: A 29-year-old man's soft tissue ultrasound shows a dark collection, and its contents move when the probe presses on it. What does this suggest?
opts: Cellulitis
Cellulitis shows distortion of soft tissue and cobblestoning, with no collection whose contents shift.
A thrombosed vein
A thrombosed vein does NOT compress, and nothing in it moves: thrombus is noncompressible.
An abscess
Correct. An abscess is an anechoic or hypoechoic collection, and pus will shift with compressing. Cellulitis distorts the tissue with cobblestoning but has no collection to move.
An artery
An artery is pulsatile with minimal compressibility. Contents shifting under pressure in a collection is pus.

set1.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Cardiovascular assessment.
set1.q: A 61-year-old man has this focused cardiac ultrasound taken from the apex, showing four chambers with the septum running vertically. Which window is it?
opts: Parasternal long axis
The parasternal long axis lays the heart lengthwise with the aorta and left atrium; it does not show all four chambers side by side.
Parasternal short axis
The parasternal short axis cuts the ventricles into a ring; it does not show four chambers at once.
Subxiphoid
The subxiphoid view looks through the liver from under the xiphoid, with the liver at the top of the image.
Apical four chamber

Correct. The apical four chamber view allows simultaneous visualization of all four chambers and is important for assessing right ventricular dilation or strain. It is sometimes a difficult view to obtain.

set1.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Abdominal assessment.
set1.q: A 41-year-old man is scanned in the right upper quadrant during an EFAST (extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma) exam. Which fluid does this window look for?
opts: Free air for a pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is looked for at the right and left anterior chest windows, not the upper quadrant windows.
Pleural free fluid alone
The upper quadrant windows look for BOTH peritoneal and pleural free fluid, not pleural fluid alone.
Peritoneal and pleural free fluid

Correct. The right and left upper quadrant windows look for peritoneal and pleural free fluid; the suprapubic window for peritoneal free fluid; the subxiphoid for pericardial effusion; the anterior chest for pneumothorax.
Pericardial fluid only
Pericardial effusion is the subxiphoid window's question; the upper quadrant windows look for peritoneal and pleural free fluid.

set1.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set1.q: A 34-year-old man has this right upper quadrant image after a fall. How is the dark stripe the arrow points to, between the liver and kidney, described?
opts: Anechoic
Correct. The stripe between the liver and kidney is black: it returns no echo, the look of fluid. Here it is free fluid in Morison's pouch. Anechoic means black and typically fluid filled.
Isoechoic
Isoechoic tissue matches its surroundings. The stripe stands out as black against the gray liver and kidney.
Hypoechoic
Hypoechoic is gray, like the liver and kidney themselves. The stripe between them is black, which is anechoic.
Hyperechoic
Hyperechoic is white, dense structures such as bone and stones. The stripe the arrow marks is black, not white.
set1.alt: Ultrasound image of the right upper quadrant with an arrow

set1.io: Interpret basic point-of-care ultrasound findings by distinguishing normal and abnormal findings.
set1.q: A 49-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain. On this gallbladder ultrasound, what do the arrows at the neck and beneath it point to?
opts: Side lobe artifact
Side lobe artifact projects echoes into the lumen without a true shadow. A bright focus with a dark band behind it is a stone.
A stone casting a shadow

Correct. A bright (hyperechoic) calculus sits at the gallbladder neck with a posterior acoustic shadow beneath it. Stones, wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid plus a sonographic Murphy sign are signs of cholecystitis.
Gallbladder wall thickening
Wall thickening is measured across the wall itself. The arrows mark a bright focus and the dark band behind it: a stone and its shadow.
Pericholecystic fluid
Pericholecystic fluid is a dark rim of fluid around the gallbladder, not a bright focus with a shadow behind it.
set1.alt: Ultrasound image of the gallbladder with two yellow arrows

set1.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Abdominal assessment.
set1.q: A 46-year-old man is about to have his inferior vena cava scanned for volume status. Where is the probe placed?
opts: Longitudinal, just right of midline
Correct. For the inferior vena cava the probe is placed longitudinally just to the right of midline, below the xiphoid. It helps determine volume status and fluid responsiveness.
Transverse, left of midline
The inferior vena cava sits to the RIGHT of midline, scanned with the probe longitudinal.
Over the cardiac apex
The apex is the window for the apical four chamber view of the heart, not the inferior vena cava.
On the anterior chest
The anterior chest windows look for pneumothorax. The inferior vena cava is scanned below the xiphoid, just right of midline.

set1.io: Discuss the role of point-of-care ultrasound as an adjunct to the history and physical examination.
set1.q: A 54-year-old woman needs ultrasound-guided intravenous access. While scanning, how does the clinician tell her artery from her vein?
opts: The vein shows blue on Doppler
On color Doppler, blue and red do not necessarily mean venous and arterial: blue is flow away from the probe, red toward it. Compression is the bedside test.
The artery compresses completely
This reverses the rule. The artery is pulsatile and barely compresses; the vein is the one that flattens completely under the probe.
The vein is the brighter structure
Brightness is echogenicity, and fluid-filled vessels are both dark. Compressibility and pulsatility tell them apart.
The vein compresses completely

Correct. In general, arteries are pulsatile and have minimal compressibility, while veins are completely compressible (unless filled with clot). Knowing this identifies structures, especially for vascular procedures.

set1.io: Interpret basic point-of-care ultrasound findings by distinguishing normal and abnormal findings.
set1.q: A 59-year-old man's leg scan shows a noncompressible vein. Why can the clot inside look dark in one patient and bright in another?
opts: Dark content means arterial flow
Dark content is not a sign of an artery. Clot may look hypoechoic or hyperechoic depending on chronicity.
Bright content means no clot
Thrombus can be hyperechoic as well as hypoechoic. A noncompressible vein holds clot whatever its brightness.
Its echogenicity depends on gain only
Gain changes the whole image's brightness. The clot's own look varies with how old it is.
Its echogenicity depends on chronicity

Correct. In a deep vein thrombosis, hypoechoic or hyperechoic content may be seen depending on chronicity, so noncompressibility, not brightness, is the major diagnostic feature. Color flow may also be lost.

set1.io: Interpret basic point-of-care ultrasound findings by distinguishing normal and abnormal findings.
set1.q: A 22-year-old man has sudden chest pain and dyspnea, and this M-mode tracing is taken over his anterior chest. Smooth horizontal lines continue below the pleural line. What does this show?
opts: Pulmonary edema
Pulmonary edema gives vertical B lines on the B-mode image, not horizontal lines down an M-mode tracing.
A pneumothorax

Correct. When smooth horizontal lines run all the way down below the pleural line, the barcode pattern, there is no moving lung against the chest wall: a pneumothorax. M-mode's common uses are pneumothorax and fetal ultrasound.
A pleural effusion
An effusion is anechoic fluid on the B-mode image, with the spine seen through it, not a barcode pattern in M-mode.
Normal lung sliding
Normal lung gives a grainy pattern below the pleural line ('sand on the beach') beneath the smooth chest wall lines ('ocean'). Lines all the way down are the barcode of pneumothorax.
set1.alt: M-mode tracing beneath a small ultrasound image

set1.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set1.q: A 48-year-old man has this right upper quadrant ultrasound. Liver-like tissue appears above the bright curved line of the diaphragm, where lung should be. What is this?
opts: Pleural effusion
Normally air above the diaphragm is an acoustic barrier, which is why the mirror appears. With an effusion, the mirroring is absent and the spine is seen instead.
Side lobe artifact
Side lobe artifact projects echoes from a strong reflector outside the beam into a structure. Liver copied across the diaphragm is a mirror image.
Mirror image artifact
Correct. Mirror image artifact is a reverberation artifact: the sound hits a strong reflector (the diaphragm) and the liver appears mirrored on the other side of it.
Edge artifact
Edge artifact is a dark refraction line off the edge of a fluid-filled structure, not a copy of the liver.
set1.alt: Ultrasound image of the liver, diaphragm and kidney

set1.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with dyspnea has this lung ultrasound. What are the vertical bright lines running from the pleura to the bottom of the screen?
opts: A lines
A lines are horizontal, evenly spaced repeats of the pleural line, the normal lung. These lines are vertical.
Comet tails
Comet tails are vertical lines too, but off calcifications, cholesterol or metal, as in a gallbladder wall. In the lung, from an air-water interface, they are B lines.
B lines
Correct. B lines are vertical hyperechoic lines in the lung from an air-water interface, seen with pulmonary edema.
Acoustic shadowing
Shadowing is a dark band behind a dense, hyperechoic structure such as a rib or stone. These lines are bright and vertical: B lines.

set1.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set1.q: A 61-year-old woman's mass looks exactly as bright as the tissue around it. How is it described?
opts: Hypoechoic
Hypoechoic is darker (gray) than the surroundings, returning less echo. A mass exactly as bright as its surroundings is isoechoic.
Hyperechoic
Hyperechoic is brighter (white) than the surroundings. Equal brightness is isoechoic.
Anechoic
Anechoic is black, returning no echo, typically fluid. Equal brightness to the surroundings is isoechoic.
Isoechoic
Correct. Isoechoic means the same density (brightness) as the surrounding structures, which is why such a lesion can blend in.

set1.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set1.q: A 68-year-old woman with a large body habitus needs a deep abdominal structure imaged. Which probe frequency fits, and at what cost?
opts: Higher: more depth and detail
No frequency gives both. Higher frequency buys resolution at the cost of depth; lower frequency buys depth at the cost of resolution.
Higher: more depth, less detail
Higher frequency gives better resolution and LESS depth. Depth comes from lower frequency.
Lower: more depth, less detail
Correct. Lower frequency probes give better depth but less resolution; higher frequency probes give better resolution but less depth.
Lower: more detail, less depth
This reverses both halves. Lower frequency trades resolution away for depth, which is why it suits a deep structure in a large patient.

set1.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set1.q: A 59-year-old woman has gallstones on ultrasound, and a dark band runs straight down beneath each stone. What is this called?
opts: Posterior acoustic enhancement
Enhancement is the reverse: sound passing through a fluid-filled structure makes the area deep to it brighter. A stone casts a dark shadow.
Mirror image artifact
Mirror image artifact duplicates a structure on the other side of a strong reflector. A dark band under a stone is a shadow.
Acoustic shadowing

Correct. Acoustic shadowing happens with hyperechoic structures such as stones and bone: little sound passes them, so the area behind is dark. Air can shadow too, looking 'dirtier' than the shadow from bone.
Edge artifact
Edge artifact is refraction, sound 'bending' off the edge of a fluid-filled structure. A dark band beneath each stone is shadowing.

set1.io: Interpret basic point-of-care ultrasound findings by distinguishing normal and abnormal findings.
set1.q: A 74-year-old woman with dyspnea has this ultrasound with the probe on her lower lateral chest. What does it show?
opts: Free fluid around the spleen
Free fluid in the left upper quadrant sits around the spleen, below the diaphragm. This collection lies above the diaphragm.
A pneumothorax
A pneumothorax is assessed over the anterior chest by lung sliding, the barcode pattern and the lung point; it is air, not a dark fluid collection.
Normal aerated lung
Normal lung above the diaphragm is an air barrier with a mirrored liver, not a dark fluid space.
A pleural effusion
Correct. The image shows a dark (anechoic) fluid collection above the bright curve of the diaphragm, the look of a pleural effusion. A curvilinear probe is the better choice for an effusion.
set1.alt: Ultrasound image of the lower chest

set1.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set1.q: A 55-year-old man has this transverse gallbladder ultrasound. What are the short vertical bright lines coming off the wall?
opts: B lines
B lines are the vertical lines of the LUNG, from an air-water interface in pulmonary edema. This is a gallbladder.
Edge artifact
Edge artifact is a dark refraction line off the edge of a fluid-filled structure. These are bright vertical tails.
Comet tails
Correct. Comet tails are reverberation artifacts, vertical hyperechoic lines off calcifications, cholesterol or metal, here trailing from the gallbladder wall.
Side lobe artifact
Side lobe artifact places echoes from a reflector outside the beam inside the lumen. These are vertical tails off the wall.
set1.alt: Ultrasound image of the gallbladder, transverse

set1.io: Interpret basic point-of-care ultrasound findings by distinguishing normal and abnormal findings.
set1.q: A 60-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain. What does the arrow beside her gallbladder point to?
opts: A gallstone
A gallstone is a bright (hyperechoic) focus with an acoustic shadow behind it, not a dark stripe outside the wall.
Pericholecystic fluid

Correct. The arrow marks a thin dark (anechoic) stripe of fluid beside the gallbladder: pericholecystic fluid, one of the signs of cholecystitis with stones, wall thickening and a sonographic Murphy sign.
Gallbladder wall thickening
Wall thickening is the wall itself grown thick. The arrow marks dark fluid outside the wall.
Shadow from bowel
Bowel gas casts its own shadow deeper in this image. The arrow marks dark fluid hugging the gallbladder.
set1.alt: Ultrasound image of the gallbladder with a white arrow

set1.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Pulmonary assessment.
set1.q: A 78-year-old man in acute respiratory failure has a BLUE (bilateral lung ultrasound in emergency) scan showing diffuse vertical hyperechoic lines on both sides. Which condition do these lines point to?
opts: Normal aerated lung
Normal aerated lung shows evenly spaced horizontal A lines. Diffuse vertical B lines are abnormal and point to pulmonary edema.
Pneumothorax
A pneumothorax shows absent lung sliding. Vertical B lines come from an air-water interface in the lung, as in pulmonary edema.
Pleural effusion
A pleural effusion is a dark (anechoic) fluid collection, not vertical bright lines in the lung.
Pulmonary edema

Correct. Vertical hyperechoic lines in the lung are B lines, from an air-water interface, and they are seen with pulmonary edema. The BLUE (bilateral lung ultrasound in emergency) protocol is one bilateral lung scanning approach.

set1.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set1.q: A 44-year-old woman is scanned for a general, non-cardiac study. Where should the probe's indicator point?
opts: To the scanner's left (her right)

Correct. The indicator (probe marker, orientation marker) orients the image and is kept pointed to your left, the patient's right; it should match the orientation marker on the display. Cardiology puts it the opposite way.
Toward her feet
The rule is a left-right one: the indicator to your left, the patient's right, matching the screen marker.
It does not matter
The indicator orients you to the image; it should match the orientation on the display screen, so its direction matters.
To the scanner's right (her left)
That is the cardiology convention, which puts the indicator opposite. For a general scan the indicator points to your left, the patient's right.

set1.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set1.q: A 26-year-old student asks how an ultrasound probe makes an image. What sends out and receives the sound waves?
opts: A magnet around the patient
There is no magnet: ultrasound uses sound. Piezoelectric crystals built into the probe both send the sound wave and convert the returning echo to electricity.
The gel itself, when warmed
The gel makes no sound. The sound comes from piezoelectric crystals vibrating when current passes through them.
An x-ray tube in the probe
Ultrasound uses no ionizing radiation. The probe's piezoelectric crystals vibrate to make sound waves and read their echoes.
Piezoelectric crystals in the probe

Correct. A current passed through tiny piezoelectric crystals in the probe makes them vibrate and send out sound; the returning echo vibrates them again, and that is converted to electricity the computer turns into a real-time image.

set1.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Cardiovascular assessment.
set1.q: A 73-year-old woman is hypotensive and a pericardial effusion is suspected. Which cardiac window is best for finding it?
opts: Apical four chamber
The apical four chamber view is important for right ventricular dilation or strain. The effusion view is subxiphoid.
Subxiphoid

Correct. The subxiphoid view is the best view for pericardial effusion, since most effusions are inferior. It uses the liver as a window, with the probe under the xiphoid just to the patient's right of midline.
Parasternal long axis
The parasternal long axis is often the easiest view to obtain, but the best view for an effusion is subxiphoid, because most effusions are inferior.
Parasternal short axis
The parasternal short axis gives a cross-section of the ventricles and a good view of the mitral and aortic valves; it is not named the best effusion view.

set2.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set2.q: A 31-year-old woman asks why she cannot hear the ultrasound machine's sound waves. What is the reason?
opts: They are below about 20 hertz
Sound below the range of hearing is the other end of the spectrum. Ultrasound is above the audible range, more than 20,000 hertz.
They are above about 20,000 hertz
Correct. Every ultrasound machine works by using sound above the frequency human ears can hear (more than 20,000 hertz) to create an image.
They are converted to light
The returning echoes are converted to electricity, which the computer turns into an image, not light. The waves are inaudible because they exceed 20,000 hertz.
They stay inside the gel
Sound travels through the body's structures and reflects back to the probe; that is how the image forms. She cannot hear it because the frequency is too high.

set2.io: Integrate laboratory, imaging, and electrocardiographic findings into clinical decision-making.
set2.q: A 68-year-old man with long-untreated hypertension becomes acutely breathless in a clinic waiting room; he has crackles in both lungs and a low oxygen saturation. A bedside lung scan shows B lines throughout both lungs. What does this combination point to?
opts: Flash pulmonary edema

Correct. Sudden dyspnea with long-untreated hypertension, diffuse crackles and diffuse B lines (vertical hyperechoic lines from an air-water interface) fits flash pulmonary edema. The scan adds a real-time answer at the bedside to the history and examination.
Pleural effusion alone
An effusion is an anechoic collection with the spine sign, not diffuse B lines with crackles.
Pneumothorax
A pneumothorax does not cause B lines throughout both lungs; diffuse B lines come from an air-water interface, as in edema.
Normal lungs
Normal lungs show horizontal A lines; diffuse vertical B lines with crackles are abnormal and point to edema.

set2.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set2.q: A 46-year-old man's bladder appears black on ultrasound. Which term describes it?
opts: Isoechoic
Isoechoic means the same density as the surrounding structures. A black, fluid-filled bladder stands out as anechoic.
Hypoechoic
Hypoechoic is gray: tissue returning less echo than its surroundings, such as the liver or spleen. A black, fluid-filled bladder is anechoic.
Hyperechoic
Hyperechoic is white: dense structures such as bone or stones returning more echoes. A black bladder is the opposite.
Anechoic
Correct. Anechoic means black: the structure does not echo sound waves back, typically because it is fluid filled, like a full bladder.

set2.io: Interpret basic point-of-care ultrasound findings by distinguishing normal and abnormal findings.
set2.q: A 71-year-old man's right upper quadrant scan shows no mirror image of the liver above the diaphragm, and his thoracic vertebrae are seen there. Why is the spine visible?
opts: The gain is turned too high
Gain is brightness. Turning it up does not reveal the spine through aerated lung; fluid does.
Fluid carries the sound past the diaphragm
Correct. Air is normally an acoustic barrier. With a pleural effusion the fluid amplifies the sound waves, so the thoracic vertebrae can be seen through the acoustic window (the spine sign).
The probe indicator is reversed
The indicator sets left-right orientation. It cannot make the spine appear above the diaphragm; an effusion does.
Air carries the sound past the diaphragm
Air is normally an acoustic BARRIER; it is why the liver is mirrored and the spine is not seen. Fluid is what lets the sound through.

set2.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set2.q: A 47-year-old woman's color Doppler shows red flow in a vessel. What does red mean?
opts: Flow perpendicular to the beam
Flow perpendicular to the beam shows as black. Red is flow toward the probe, blue away from it.
Flow away from the probe
Flow away from the probe is blue (BART: blue away, red towards). Red is flow toward the probe.
Arterial blood
Blue and red do not necessarily mean venous and arterial. Red is flow toward the probe.
Flow toward the probe
Correct. Color Doppler detects direction and velocity and represents them by color: BART, blue away, red towards. Blue and red do not necessarily mean venous and arterial.

set2.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set2.q: A 49-year-old woman is being scanned and the structure of interest sits off the bottom of the screen. Which control changes how far the image is zoomed in?
opts: M-mode
M-mode shows one line of the image moving over time. It is a different mode, not the zoom control.
The indicator
The indicator (probe marker) orients the image left to right; it does not change how deep the image reaches.
Depth
Correct. Depth is how far you are zoomed in; gain is brightness. Changing the depth brings a deeper structure onto the screen.
Gain
Gain is brightness. It makes the image lighter or darker but does not change how far in you are zoomed.

set2.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Pulmonary assessment.
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with pneumonia has a lung ultrasound. Which group lists findings that fit pneumonia?
opts: Bronchograms, B lines, hepatization
Correct. Pneumonia findings on ultrasound: bronchograms (air, fluid or consolidation in the bronchi), B lines, hepatization (lung looks like liver), pleural effusions or empyema, and the spine sign.
A lines, lung sliding, seashore
A lines, lung sliding and the seashore pattern are the NORMAL lung, not pneumonia. Pneumonia shows bronchograms, B lines and hepatization.
Cobblestoning and shifting pus
Cobblestoning is cellulitis and shifting pus is an abscess, both soft tissue findings.
Barcode, lung point, no sliding
The barcode pattern, a lung point and absent sliding are the findings of pneumothorax.

set2.io: Discuss the role of point-of-care ultrasound as an adjunct to the history and physical examination.
set2.q: A 33-year-old man has a painful, swollen scrotum after an injury, and his clinician considers a bedside scan. How does scrotal imaging fit point-of-care ultrasound?
opts: It is a listed contraindication
The contraindications are few: globe rupture, delaying lifesaving measures and locations not amenable to ultrasound. Scrotal assessment is on the indication list.
It needs computed tomography first
Nothing makes computed tomography a prerequisite; scrotal assessment is itself a listed point-of-care ultrasound indication.
It is a listed indication

Correct. The listed point-of-care indications are trauma, cardiac, pulmonary, vasculature, ophthalmic, renal, gallbladder, appendix, scrotal and obstetric/gynecologic. Scrotal assessment is one of them.
It is limited to abdominal organs
Point-of-care indications reach well beyond the abdomen: trauma, heart, lungs, vessels, eye, kidney, gallbladder, appendix, scrotum and obstetric/gynecologic.

set2.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Cardiovascular assessment.
set2.q: A 60-year-old man's clinician rotates the probe from the apical four chamber view to add the aortic valve and left ventricular outflow tract. What is the new view called?
opts: Subxiphoid view
The subxiphoid view is taken from under the xiphoid, using the liver as a window. The apical rotation adding the aortic valve is the five chamber view.
Parasternal long axis
The parasternal long axis is taken beside the sternum. The apical rotation adding the aortic valve is the five chamber view.
Five chamber view
Correct. From the apical four chamber view, the probe can be rotated to get a 'five chamber view' that includes the aortic valve and left ventricular outflow tract.
Parasternal short axis
The parasternal short axis comes from the parasternal long axis rotated 90 degrees, not from the apex.

set2.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Cardiovascular assessment.
set2.q: A 55-year-old man with sudden dyspnea needs his right ventricle checked for dilation or strain. Which window is important for that?
opts: Parasternal long axis
The parasternal long axis runs lengthwise through the left heart, aorta and left atrium; right ventricular dilation or strain is assessed apically.
Subxiphoid
The subxiphoid view is best for pericardial effusion, since most effusions are inferior.
Parasternal short axis
The parasternal short axis is the cross-section with a good view of the mitral and aortic valves.
Apical four chamber
Correct. The apical four chamber view shows all four chambers at once and is important for assessing right ventricular dilation or strain.

set2.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Cardiovascular assessment.
set2.q: A 52-year-old woman has this focused cardiac ultrasound, with the probe under the xiphoid and the liver across the top of the image. Which window is it?
opts: Parasternal short axis
The parasternal short axis cuts the ventricles into a ring from beside the sternum, not through the liver.
Subxiphoid
Correct. The subxiphoid (subcostal) view places the probe under the xiphoid, just to the patient's right of midline, and uses the liver as a window to view the heart.
Apical four chamber
The apical four chamber view is taken from the apex with the chambers side by side and the septum vertical, not through the liver.
Parasternal long axis
The parasternal long axis is taken beside the sternum and lays the heart out lengthwise, with no liver in the way.

set2.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman's ultrasound shows a gallstone as a bright white focus. Which term describes the stone?
opts: Hyperechoic
Correct. Hyperechoic is white: dense structures such as bone and stones return more echoes than the surrounding structures.
Isoechoic
Isoechoic tissue matches its surroundings in density. A bright stone is clearly denser, so it is hyperechoic.
Anechoic
Anechoic is black, the look of fluid that echoes nothing back. A stone is dense and white.
Hypoechoic
Hypoechoic is gray, tissue such as the liver or spleen that returns less echo than its surroundings. A stone returns more.

set2.io: Interpret basic point-of-care ultrasound findings by distinguishing normal and abnormal findings.
set2.q: A 24-year-old woman is hypotensive after a car crash. This right upper quadrant image shows a dark stripe between the liver and kidney. What does it show?
opts: Free fluid in Morison's pouch

Correct. A dark (anechoic) stripe between the liver and kidney is free fluid in Morison's pouch. The right upper quadrant window of the EFAST (extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma) exam looks for exactly this.
A normal liver-kidney interface
With no free fluid, the liver and kidney lie against each other with no dark stripe between them.
A pleural effusion
A pleural effusion lies ABOVE the diaphragm, with the spine visible through it. This stripe is between the liver and kidney, below the diaphragm.
Posterior acoustic enhancement
Enhancement is a BRIGHTER area behind fluid. The stripe here is dark: the fluid itself.
set2.alt: Ultrasound image of the right upper quadrant

set2.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Abdominal assessment.
set2.q: A 32-year-old man is hypotensive after a motorcycle crash. In the EFAST (extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma) exam, what does the subxiphoid window look for?
opts: Peritoneal free fluid
Peritoneal free fluid is looked for in the upper quadrants and the suprapubic window.
A pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is looked for at the right and left anterior chest windows, not the subxiphoid window.
A pericardial effusion

Correct. In the EFAST (extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma) windows, the subxiphoid view looks for a pericardial effusion; the right and left upper quadrants for peritoneal and pleural free fluid; the suprapubic window for peritoneal free fluid; the anterior chest for pneumothorax.
A deep vein thrombosis
A deep vein thrombosis is not part of the trauma windows; it is checked by compressing the leg veins.

mis.A pneumothorax: other EFAST (extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma) window
mis.Peritoneal free fluid: other EFAST (extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma) windows

set2.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set2.q: A 53-year-old man's gallbladder wall shows short vertical bright lines trailing from small calcifications. What are these?
opts: B lines
B lines are also vertical hyperechoic lines, but in the LUNG, from an air-water interface, seen with pulmonary edema. These trail from calcifications.
A lines
A lines are horizontal reverberations of the pleural line in the normal lung, not vertical lines off calcifications.
Acoustic shadowing
Shadowing is a dark band behind a dense structure. Vertical BRIGHT lines off calcifications are comet tails.
Comet tails
Correct. Comet tails are reverberation artifacts: vertical hyperechoic lines that may come off calcifications, cholesterol, metal and the like.

set2.io: Interpret basic point-of-care ultrasound findings by distinguishing normal and abnormal findings.
set2.q: A 63-year-old woman has a swollen leg, and the bedside scan finds a femoral vein that does not flatten when the probe presses on it. What does this mean?
opts: It is really an artery
Arteries are pulsatile with minimal compressibility, but the question names the femoral vein. A vein that will not compress is thrombosed.
A thrombus is present
Correct. Assess for compressibility: thrombus will not be compressible, the major diagnostic feature of a deep vein thrombosis. Normal veins are completely compressible.
The vein is normal
A normal vein is completely compressible. A vein that will not flatten holds a thrombus.
More gain is needed
Gain is brightness. Compressibility is a mechanical test, and failure to compress is the finding.

set2.io: Interpret basic point-of-care ultrasound findings by distinguishing normal and abnormal findings.
set2.q: A 37-year-old man is scanned in the left upper quadrant after a fall. What does the arrow point to?
opts: A normal splenic edge
A normal spleen meets the diaphragm and kidney with no dark collection beside it. The arrow marks fluid.
A kidney cyst
The kidney is labeled separately below. The arrow marks a dark collection at the splenic edge, free fluid.
Mirror image of the lung
Lung mirrored across the diaphragm is the normal above-diaphragm artifact. The arrow marks a dark collection at the spleen.
Free fluid near the spleen

Correct. The arrow marks dark (anechoic) fluid at the edge of the spleen. The left upper quadrant window of the EFAST (extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma) exam looks for peritoneal and pleural free fluid.
set2.alt: Ultrasound image of the left upper quadrant with an arrow

set2.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set2.q: A 64-year-old man has this right upper quadrant ultrasound. Which artifact appears deep to the bright foci at the neck of the dark, oval structure?
opts: Posterior acoustic enhancement
Enhancement makes the area behind a FLUID-filled structure brighter. The band behind the bright foci is dark, a shadow.
Acoustic shadowing
Correct. The bright foci are stones (hyperechoic), and the dark band running straight down behind them is acoustic shadowing: little sound gets past a dense structure.
Side lobe artifact
Side lobe artifact places echoes from a strong reflector outside the beam inside a structure. A dark band directly behind stones is shadowing.
Ring down artifact
Ring down artifact is caused by foci of air and appears as bright streaks, not a dark band under dense foci.
set2.alt: Ultrasound image of the right upper quadrant

set2.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Soft tissue assessment.
set2.q: A 40-year-old man has a red, warm, swollen forearm. His soft tissue ultrasound looks like this. Which finding is shown?
opts: Cobblestoning of cellulitis
Correct. Cellulitis distorts the soft tissue and gives a cobblestone pattern: bright fat broken up by dark lines of fluid. An abscess would instead be a discrete anechoic or hypoechoic collection.
Normal soft tissue
Normal soft tissue has orderly, undistorted layers. Distortion and cobblestoning mean cellulitis.
An abscess
An abscess is a discrete anechoic or hypoechoic collection whose pus shifts with compression, not a diffuse pattern.
A deep vein thrombosis
A deep vein thrombosis is a noncompressible vein, assessed by compression and color flow, not a pattern in the subcutaneous tissue.
set2.alt: Ultrasound image of the subcutaneous tissue

set2.io: Discuss the role of point-of-care ultrasound as an adjunct to the history and physical examination.
set2.q: A 29-year-old man has blunt trauma to the face, and an open globe rupture is suspected. Which statement about point-of-care ultrasound of that eye is true?
opts: Eye scans are not an indication
Ophthalmic scanning is on the list of point-of-care indications. What rules it out here is the suspected globe rupture, a listed contraindication.
It is a listed contraindication

Correct. Point-of-care ultrasound is not often contraindicated, but globe rupture is one of the listed contraindications. The others: it should not delay lifesaving measures, and some anatomical locations are not amenable to ultrasound.
It is safe once lifesaving care starts
Not delaying lifesaving measures is a separate contraindication. A suspected globe rupture is its own listed contraindication, whatever else is happening.
No contraindications exist
Contraindications are uncommon ('not very often'), but they exist: globe rupture, delaying lifesaving measures, and locations not amenable to ultrasound.

set2.io: Interpret basic point-of-care ultrasound findings by distinguishing normal and abnormal findings.
set2.q: A 56-year-old man has right upper quadrant pain and fever. What does the double-headed arrow on his gallbladder ultrasound measure?
opts: Wall thickening
Correct. The arrow spans the gallbladder wall, which is thickened. Wall thickening, stones and pericholecystic fluid, plus a sonographic Murphy sign, are signs of cholecystitis.
A gallstone
A gallstone is a bright focus inside the lumen with an acoustic shadow behind it. The arrow spans the wall.
The common bile duct
No duct is marked on this image. The double-headed arrow spans the gallbladder wall, which is thickened.
Pericholecystic fluid
Pericholecystic fluid is dark fluid outside the wall. The arrow measures the wall itself.
set2.alt: Ultrasound image of the gallbladder with a yellow double-headed arrow

set2.io: Interpret basic point-of-care ultrasound findings by distinguishing normal and abnormal findings.
set2.q: A 31-year-old woman has chest pain after a fall, and this M-mode tracing is recorded over her anterior chest. The pattern below the pleural line is grainy, unlike the smooth lines above it. What does it indicate?
opts: Pulmonary edema
Pulmonary edema shows as vertical B lines on the B-mode image. This M-mode pattern answers the pneumothorax question.
A pleural effusion
An effusion is anechoic fluid seen on the B-mode image, with the spine visible through it. M-mode over the anterior chest is used here for pneumothorax.
No pneumothorax

Correct. In M-mode the motionless chest wall above the pleural line makes smooth horizontal lines ('ocean') and the moving lung below it makes a grainy pattern ('sand on the beach'): the lung is against the chest wall, so there is no pneumothorax.
A pneumothorax
A pneumothorax replaces the grainy pattern below the pleural line with smooth horizontal lines all the way down, the barcode pattern.
set2.alt: M-mode tracing beneath a small ultrasound image

set2.io: Distinguish between focused point-of-care ultrasound and comprehensive ultrasonography.
set2.q: A 44-year-old woman has had one swollen, tender calf for five days after a long flight. She has no chest pain or shortness of breath and her vital signs are normal. Which study best fits?
opts: A bedside point-of-care scan
A stable patient with a likely deep vein thrombosis has time for the comprehensive study. Point-of-care ultrasound is for real-time answers when the bedside question cannot wait.
A focused cardiac scan for strain
She has no chest pain or shortness of breath. The question here is the leg veins, and in a stable patient that belongs to a formal ultrasound.
No ultrasound until symptoms worsen
A likely deep vein thrombosis still needs imaging. Stability changes which ultrasound (formal rather than point-of-care), not whether to image.
A formal venous ultrasound

Correct. A likely deep vein thrombosis in a stable patient needs a formal ultrasound; it is probably not a point-of-care question. Point-of-care scanning earns its place when an unstable or undifferentiated patient needs a bedside answer now.

set2.io: Integrate laboratory, imaging, and electrocardiographic findings into clinical decision-making.
set2.q: A 74-year-old man is hypotensive after days of diarrhea. His bedside scan shows the inferior vena cava collapsing by more than half with inspiration. How does this guide his care?
opts: The scan cannot assess volume
Assessing volume status and fluid responsiveness is exactly what the inferior vena cava scan is for.
He is likely fluid responsive

Correct. The inferior vena cava helps determine volume status and fluid responsiveness; collapse of more than 50% with inspiration is indicative of dehydration or fluid responsiveness, which fits his history.
He is volume overloaded
Marked collapse with inspiration points the other way: dehydration or fluid responsiveness.
He has a pericardial effusion
An effusion is looked for in the subxiphoid cardiac view; collapse of the inferior vena cava speaks to volume.

set2.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set2.q: A 39-year-old woman is scanned with the probe across her abdomen and the indicator to the scanner's left, looking up through her from the feet. What is this plane?
opts: Sagittal (longitudinal)
The sagittal or longitudinal plane runs along the body's long axis. A probe across the abdomen with the indicator to your left is the transverse view.
Coronal (frontal)
The coronal or frontal plane is taken from the side of the body. Across the abdomen, indicator to your left, is transverse.
Transverse (axial)
Correct. The transverse or axial plane is scanned with the indicator to your left, looking through the patient. The other two planes are sagittal (longitudinal) and coronal (frontal).
Oblique (parasternal)
Parasternal is a cardiac window, not one of the three planes (transverse, sagittal, coronal).

set2.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Abdominal assessment.
set2.q: A 45-year-old woman's bedside scan shows gallstones, a thickened gallbladder wall and pericholecystic fluid. Which added finding completes the ultrasound signs of cholecystitis?
opts: A collapsing inferior vena cava
Collapse of the inferior vena cava of more than half with inspiration points to dehydration or fluid responsiveness, not cholecystitis.
Posterior acoustic enhancement
Enhancement is the brightening behind any fluid-filled structure, including a normal gallbladder. It is not a sign of cholecystitis.
A lines over the right lung
A lines are the normal lung's reverberation pattern; they say nothing about the gallbladder.
A sonographic Murphy sign
Correct. Stones, wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid, plus a sonographic Murphy sign, are the signs of cholecystitis on ultrasound.

set2.io: Discuss common point-of-care ultrasound applications in: Pulmonary assessment.
set2.q: A 77-year-old woman with orthopnea and leg swelling has this lung ultrasound. Which condition do the vertical bright lines point to?
opts: Pleural effusion
A pleural effusion is a dark (anechoic) fluid collection with the spine seen through it, not vertical bright lines.
Normal aerated lung
Normal lung shows horizontal A lines with lung sliding, not vertical B lines. Vertical B lines point to pulmonary edema.
Pulmonary edema
Correct. These are B lines: vertical hyperechoic lines in the lung from an air-water interface, seen with pulmonary edema.
Pneumothorax
A pneumothorax has no lung against the chest wall: no sliding, a barcode in M-mode, a lung point. B lines arise from the lung itself, so they argue against it.

set2.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set2.q: A 42-year-old woman has this lung ultrasound. What are the evenly spaced horizontal bright lines deep to the pleura?
opts: Rib shadows
Rib shadows are dark bands beneath the ribs from acoustic shadowing. The lines asked about are bright and horizontal.
Comet tails
Comet tails are vertical hyperechoic lines off calcifications, cholesterol or metal. These are horizontal repeats of the pleura.
A lines
Correct. A lines are reverberation artifacts: evenly spaced horizontal bright lines repeating the pleural line, the normal lung pattern.
B lines
B lines are VERTICAL hyperechoic lines from an air-water interface, seen with pulmonary edema. These lines are horizontal.
set2.alt: Ultrasound image of the chest wall and lung

mis.Rib shadows: adjacent artifact on the same image

set2.io: Employ established ultrasound terminology to communicate findings effectively.
set2.q: A 50-year-old woman has this ultrasound of a fluid-filled oval structure. What does the red arrow at its edge show?
opts: Edge artifact
Correct. Edge artifact is a refraction artifact: sound waves 'bend' off the edge of a fluid-filled structure, leaving a dark line running down from its edge, where the arrow points.
Mirror image artifact
Mirror image artifact duplicates structures on the other side of a strong reflector such as the diaphragm. This is a line off the edge of a fluid-filled structure.
Posterior acoustic enhancement
Enhancement brightens the area BEHIND the fluid. The arrow marks a dark line off its edge.
Acoustic shadowing from a stone
Shadowing hangs beneath a bright, hyperechoic stone. Here there is no stone; the dark line starts at the curved edge of the fluid-filled structure.
set2.alt: Ultrasound image of a fluid-filled oval structure with a red arrow

set2.io: Distinguish between focused point-of-care ultrasound and comprehensive ultrasonography.
set2.q: A 38-year-old woman's bedside ultrasound in the emergency department suggests gallbladder disease. What may still be needed after this point-of-care scan?
opts: Formal imaging to follow

Correct. Point-of-care ultrasound is a complement to the rest of the workup, and it may often still need formal imaging to follow. It answers a focused question fast; it does not replace the comprehensive study.
A radiologist to re-read the clip
The bedside scan is interpreted by the provider who performs it. What may follow is formal imaging (a comprehensive study by a sonographer, read by a radiologist), not a re-read of the bedside clip.
Nothing: it replaces formal imaging
Point-of-care ultrasound is focused and limited. It complements the workup, and formal imaging may often still need to follow it, so it does not replace the comprehensive study.
A repeat scan by the same clinician
Repeating the same focused scan answers the same narrow question again. What may still need to follow is formal, comprehensive imaging.

mis.A repeat scan by the same clinician: does not add the comprehensive study
